nameStory: The Eastern Saltmarsh Woodlouse gets its name from its favorite hangout spot – the salty marshes along our Atlantic coast. Unlike most woodlice that avoid salt like the plague, this little crustacean has made saltwater its specialty, earning it a unique place in the woodlouse world.
description: This is a small, oval-shaped crustacean that looks like a tiny armadillo, measuring about half an inch long. Despite being called a "woodlouse," it's actually more closely related to shrimp and crabs than to insects. Its segmented body is typically grayish-brown and can roll into a protective ball when threatened. You'll find this hardy little creature scuttling around saltmarshes where most other woodlice simply can't survive.

idTips.label: Saltmarsh habitat
idTips.description: Found exclusively in salty environments near the coast – if you're finding woodlice in a saltmarsh, this is likely your species

idTips.label: Body texture
idTips.description: Feels smooth and hard like a tiny piece of armor when gently touched, with distinct segments you can feel with your finger

idTips.label: Rolling behavior
idTips.description: Curls into a tight ball when disturbed, making a satisfying clicking sound as the segments lock together

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: About the size of a small pill or your pinky nail, typically around half an inch long

idTips.label: Color pattern
idTips.description: Grayish-brown with slightly darker bands across the segments, giving it a striped appearance

idTips.label: Hiding spots
idTips.description: Found under boards, driftwood, and debris that feels damp and smells slightly briny

habitat: Look for these hardy crustaceans in saltmarshes along New England's coast, particularly under wooden boards, driftwood, and other debris near the high tide line. They thrive in areas where salt spray reaches and the ground stays consistently moist with brackish water. You'll often find them in association with salt-tolerant plants like cordgrass and sea lavender.

seasonality.spring: Most active as temperatures warm up, often found under debris that's been softened by winter storms and spring rains.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when you're most likely to spot them scurrying around during cooler morning and evening hours.
seasonality.fall: Still active but beginning to seek deeper shelter under logs and boards as temperatures drop.
seasonality.winter: Hidden deep under protective debris and in soil crevices, rarely seen on the surface except during unusually warm spells.

funFact: This is one of the few woodlice in North America that has completely adapted to living in salty conditions that would kill most of its freshwater relatives – it's basically the marine biologist of the woodlouse world!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with common pill bugs (roly-polies), but remember the simple rule: if it's in a saltmarsh, it's probably the saltmarsh woodlouse, since regular pill bugs can't handle the salt. Regular woodlice also tend to be more uniformly colored without the subtle striping.
contextualKnowledge: Don't let the name "woodlouse" fool you – these aren't insects at all, but actually crustaceans more closely related to lobsters and crabs. The "louse" part of the name is just an old-fashioned way of saying "small crawling creature" and has nothing to do with parasitic lice.
compareHints: Since this is the only species in its genus found in New England, compare it to other coastal woodlice by its exclusive saltmarsh habitat and striped appearance. Most other woodlice in our region stick to freshwater environments and lack the distinctive banding pattern across their segments.
